tasks.description: Define a class `Dog` with an `__init__` method that takes `name` and `breed`. Create an instance and print the dog's name.
tasks.hint:
`class Dog:` defines a new class (by convention, class names are CamelCase).
`def __init__(self, name, breed):` runs automatically when you create an instance.
Store attributes: `self.name = name` — `self` refers to the specific instance being created.
tasks.walkthrough:
Calling `Dog('Rex', 'labrador')` runs `__init__` with `self` set to the new object.
The two values are stored as attributes, and `my_dog.name` reads one back.

tasks.description: Add a method `bark()` to the Dog class that prints '{name} says: Woof!'. Call it on your Dog instance.
tasks.hint:
Methods are functions inside a class — they always take `self` as first parameter.
`def bark(self):` — access the dog's name with `self.name`.
Call it on an instance: `my_dog.bark()` — Python passes `self` automatically.
tasks.walkthrough:
`bark` is indented inside the class, at the same level as `__init__`.
When you call `my_dog.bark()`, Python passes `my_dog` in as `self`, so `self.name` is Rex.

tasks.description: Add a `__str__` method to Dog that returns 'Dog: {name} ({breed})'. Print the Dog instance directly.
tasks.hint:
`__str__` is the 'string representation' — Python calls it automatically when you `print()` an object.
It must `return` a string (not print one).
Once defined, `print(my_dog)` calls `__str__` and prints the returned string.
tasks.walkthrough:
`print` asks the object for its string form by calling `__str__`.
The method returns a formatted string, which is what gets displayed.

tasks.description: Create a class `Rectangle` with `width` and `height`. Add an `area()` method and a `perimeter()` method. Test with width=5, height=3.
tasks.hint:
`self.width = width` and `self.height = height` in `__init__`.
`def area(self): return self.width * self.height`
`def perimeter(self): return 2 * (self.width + self.height)`
Create: `r = Rectangle(5, 3)` then `print(f'Area: {r.area()}')` etc.
tasks.walkthrough:
Both methods use the stored width and height through `self`.
The output lines are labelled to match the expected output exactly: `Area: 15` and `Perimeter: 16`.

tasks.description: Create a class `Counter` with a count starting at 0. Add increment() and reset() methods and a get_count() method. Test: increment 3 times, get count, reset, get count.
tasks.hint:
`self.count = 0` in `__init__`.
`increment()`: `self.count += 1`, `reset()`: `self.count = 0`, `get_count()`: `return self.count`
Call in order: `c.increment()` x3, `print(c.get_count())`, `c.reset()`, `print(c.get_count())`
tasks.walkthrough:
The count lives on the object as `self.count`, starting at 0.
Three increments bring it to 3, `reset` puts it back to 0, and `get_count` reports the value each time.

tasks.description: Create a class `BankAccount` with a balance. Add deposit(amount) and withdraw(amount) methods. Withdraw should not allow the balance to go below 0. Test: deposit 100, withdraw 30, withdraw 200, print balance.
tasks.hint:
`self.balance = 0` in `__init__`.
`deposit(self, amount): self.balance += amount`
`withdraw`: check `if amount > self.balance: print('Insufficient funds')` else subtract.
After deposit(100), withdraw(30), withdraw(200): balance should be 70.
tasks.walkthrough:
`withdraw` checks the amount against the balance before subtracting, so the balance can never go negative.
100 in, 30 out leaves 70. The attempt to take 200 is refused, so the final balance is still 70.

lesson.intro:
A class is a blueprint for a kind of thing: a dog, a bank account, a rectangle.
It bundles data (the dog's name) with the functions that work on that data
(bark). Once you've written the blueprint you can make as many objects from it
as you like. This is the start of object-oriented programming.

sections.heading: A class with __init__
sections.body:
`__init__` is a special method that runs automatically when you create an
object. `self` is the object being created. `self.name = name` stores the
value on the object so other methods can use it later.

Class names are capitalised by convention. You create an object by calling
the class like a function.
sections.code:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.name = name
        self.breed = breed

rex = Dog('Rex', 'labrador')
print(rex.name)
print(rex.breed)

sections.heading: Methods
sections.body:
A method is a function defined inside the class. Its first parameter is
always `self`, and Python fills that in for you when you call
`rex.bark()`. Inside the method, `self.name` is this particular dog's name.
sections.output:
Rex says: Woof!
Bella says: Woof!

sections.heading: __str__: what print shows
sections.body:
Printing an object normally shows something unhelpful like
`<__main__.Dog object at 0x...>`. Define `__str__` to return a string and
`print` will use it.

sections.heading: Objects that change over time
sections.body:
Attributes can be updated by methods. Each object keeps its own copy, so two
counters don't interfere with each other.
sections.code:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1

a = Counter()
b = Counter()
a.increment()
a.increment()
b.increment()
print(a.count, b.count)

watch_out: Forgetting `self` as the first parameter of a method. Python then complains about the number of arguments.
Writing `name = name` inside `__init__` instead of `self.name = name`. Without `self.` the value is lost when `__init__` ends.
`__init__` has two underscores on each side.
`__str__` must return a string, not print one.
